title: Collocation and precision
summary: After this unit you can choose natural verb-noun and adjective-noun partnerships, precise intensifiers and the right near-synonym, as band 9 writers and speakers do.

items.title: Collocation is what examiners mean by 'natural'
body: The band 9 descriptor for Lexical Resource mentions 'very natural and sophisticated control of lexical features'. In practice, the most common thing that makes C1 writing sound non-native is not a rare word missing but a **verb-noun partnership** that native writers would never use: *make a research*, *do a mistake*, *rise a question*.
Learn nouns together with the two or three verbs that habitually go with them. The pairs below are the backbone of Task 2 argument.
list: an argument: **put forward / advance / support / undermine** an argument
evidence: **gather / provide / weigh up**; evidence **suggests / points to**
a policy: **introduce / implement / adopt / scrap** a policy
a problem: **address / tackle / exacerbate / alleviate** a problem
a question: **raise / pose / address** a question
a decision: **make / reach / take** a decision (British English often says *take*)
pressure: **put / exert** pressure on; **come under** pressure

items.title: Verbs that sharpen an argument
body: Weak verbs (*make*, *do*, *give*, *have*, *get*) are not wrong, but precise verbs carry more meaning and earn Lexical Resource. Compare *This gives problems for farmers* with *This poses difficulties for farmers* or *This places farmers under strain*.

examples.text: The new law will make the housing shortage worse. / The new law will exacerbate the housing shortage.
examples.note: One precise verb replaces a phrase.

examples.text: The study gives evidence that... / The study provides evidence that...
examples.note: provide is the standard collocation with evidence.

examples.text: This idea has some problems. / This argument does not withstand scrutiny.

items.q: Choose the natural collocation: 'Critics have ___ several objections to the scheme.'
items.why: We *raise* objections, questions and concerns. *Risen* is intransitive (*prices have risen*) and cannot take an object.

items.q: Choose the natural collocation: 'Governments must ___ the problem of food waste.'
items.why: *Tackle* or *address* a problem is standard. Phrasal-looking forms like *solve out* do not exist.

items.text: The evidence ___ to a clear link between sleep and academic performance.
items.why: *The evidence points to* a conclusion is a fixed academic collocation.

items.text: Several countries have already ___ policies that limit single-use plastic.
items.why: Governments *introduce*, *adopt* or *implement* policies.

items.text: Rising rents have put enormous ___ on young families.
items.why: *Put pressure / strain on* someone is a natural verb-noun collocation.

items.text: Parents play a crucial ___ in shaping children's attitudes to reading.
items.why: *Play a role / part in* is the standard collocation.

items.q: Match each noun with its most natural verb.
items.why: Pose a threat; weigh up evidence; reach a compromise; scrap a tax (informal-neutral British English for abolish); undermine trust.

options: The council did a decision to close the library.
The council took the decision to close the library.
The council made up a decision to close the library.
The council gave a decision to close the library.
items.why: *Take* or *make* a decision. *Do* and *give* do not collocate with *decision*; *make up* means *invent* or *compensate*.

items.q: 'This would make the situation worse.' Which is the most precise upgrade?
options: This would worsen up the situation.
This would do the situation bad.
items.why: *Exacerbate* means 'make (a problem) worse', and collocates naturally with *situation*, *problem* and *tension*.

items.q: Order the words to make a natural sentence.
items.why: *Lend weight to an argument* is a strong academic collocation; *considerable* intensifies it naturally.

items.title: Adjective + noun
body: English chooses adjectives for nouns in ways that logic does not predict. We say *heavy traffic* but not *strong traffic*, *high unemployment* but not *big unemployment*, *a strong argument* but not *a powerful reason* (though *a powerful argument* is fine).
These partnerships are worth learning in sets.
list: **heavy**: traffic, rain, losses, reliance on, burden

items.title: Adverb + adjective intensifiers
body: *Very* is fine in speech but weak in writing. Precise intensifiers collocate with specific adjectives: *highly* goes with words of probability and value, *deeply* with feelings and beliefs, *bitterly* with disappointment and cold, *widely* with knowledge and acceptance.
items.tip: Non-gradable adjectives (*essential*, *impossible*, *unique*) take *absolutely*, *completely* or *virtually*, not *very*: *virtually impossible*, not *very impossible*.

items.q: Choose the natural collocation: 'There is ___ concern about the cost of living.'
items.why: *Widespread concern* is the standard collocation; *wide concern* is unusual.

items.q: Choose the natural collocation: 'The policy proved ___ unpopular with voters.'
items.why: *Deeply unpopular* is the most natural pairing; *highly* tends to go with *likely*, *effective* or *controversial*.

items.text: It is highly ___ that the scheme will be ready on time; it is already six months behind.
items.why: *Highly unlikely* is a fixed collocation for low probability.

items.text: The city is notorious for its ___ traffic during the morning rush hour.
items.why: *Heavy traffic*, not *strong* or *big traffic*.

items.text: There is a growing ___ of evidence that green spaces improve mental health.
items.why: *A growing body of evidence* is a common academic collocation.

items.text: Without public transport, getting to the hospital from the village is ___ impossible.
items.why: *Impossible* is non-gradable, so it takes *virtually* or *almost*, not *very*.

items.q: Choose the best intensifier for each adjective.

rows.label: ___ regarded as the best in the country

items.why: bitterly disappointed, fully aware, widely regarded, deeply rooted, highly controversial.

options: There was a big rise of unemployment in the region.
There was a sharp rise in unemployment in the region.
There was a strong rise in the unemployment of the region.
There was a heavy rise in unemployment in the region.
items.why: *A sharp rise in* is the standard collocation and preposition. *Big rise of* has a weak adjective and the wrong preposition.

items.q: Which sentence would sound most natural in a Task 2 essay?
options: This is a very essential step.
This is an absolutely essential step.
This is a highly essential step.
This is a deeply essential step.
items.why: *Essential* is non-gradable, so it takes *absolutely*, not *very*, *highly* or *deeply*.

items.title: Words that are not quite interchangeable
body: At band 9, word choice is precise: the examiner should never have to guess which of two meanings you intended. Many confusions come from near-synonyms that differ in grammar, connotation or register.
list: **affect** (verb) vs **effect** (noun; as a verb it means *bring about*: *effect change*)
**problem** (difficulty) vs **issue** (topic of debate, or a problem) vs **challenge** (difficulty to overcome, positive connotation)
**lead to** (result in) vs **cause** (direct agent, often negative)

items.title: Connotation and stance
body: Some synonyms differ mainly in attitude. *Thrifty* and *mean* describe the same behaviour, approvingly and disapprovingly. In an argument essay, choosing the word with the right connotation is a way of showing stance without saying *I think*.

examples.text: Supporters call it an *investment*; critics call it an *expense*.
The policy was *ambitious*. / The policy was *unrealistic*.
examples.note: Positive vs negative evaluation of the same scale of plan.
modest = small but meaningful; negligible = too small to matter.

items.q: 'The new rules will ___ thousands of small businesses.'
items.why: *Affect* is the verb meaning 'have an influence on'. *Effect* as a verb means 'bring about' (*effect change*).

items.q: 'The government has decided to ___ the minimum wage.'
items.why: *Raise* takes an object (*raise the wage*); *rise* does not (*the wage rose*).

items.q: 'The company's ___ performance has improved this year.'
items.why: *Economic* relates to the economy or finances. *Economical* means using money or resources efficiently (*an economical car*).

items.text: The change was so small that its effect on prices was ___; nobody noticed it.
items.why: *Negligible* means too small to be worth considering, which matches 'nobody noticed it'.

items.text: This trend is worrying, ___ for young people entering the job market.
items.why: *Especially* (= particularly). *Specially* means 'for a specific purpose' (*specially designed*).

items.text: Learning a language as an adult is a ___, but a rewarding one.
items.why: *Challenge* suits a difficulty that is worth overcoming; *problem* would not fit 'a rewarding one'.

items.q: Choose the word with the right meaning or connotation.

rows.label: Supporters praised the ___ targets as a sign of real commitment.
Critics dismissed the same targets as ___, given the budget.
The scheme produced a ___ but worthwhile improvement in attendance.
The cost per household was ___, less than a penny a year.

items.why: *Ambitious* praises a bold plan; *unrealistic* criticises it. *Modest* means small but meaningful; *negligible* means too small to matter.

options: My car has an issue with its brakes, so I'm issuing it to a garage.
Immigration is one of the most divisive issues in the election.
I have an issue of eight children.
items.why: *Issue* fits a topic of public debate. In A the verb is misused, in C the meaning is wrong, and D's 'issue' is too vague to rise.

options: Less people drive to work than ten years ago.
Fewer people drive to work than ten years ago.
Littler people drive to work than ten years ago.
Fewer traffic is seen than ten years ago.
items.why: *Fewer* with countable plurals (*people*); *less* with uncountables (*less traffic*).

items.q: Order the words to make a precise sentence.
items.why: *Is likely to lead to* hedges a causal claim; *a modest fall* states the size precisely.
